bearings.paper_claim: Senate seats are filled by two party mechanisms. Republicans use a seniority-ordered Serial Dictatorship that the paper says seems to be run as TTC/YRMH-IGYT in practice. Democrats use a Boston approximation with COC tie-breaking. Cross-party seniority-at-appointment gaps on some committees are read as possible party discipline: Environment and Public Works R mean 3.80 (N=30) vs D 1.00 (N=14), diff 2.80, t=3.05; Commerce, Science and Transport diff -1.74, t=-2.09; 104th-114th.
bearings.paper_location: Sec. 3.1-3.3 pp. 7-9; Sec. 3.5.1 p. 13 (TTC in practice); Sec. 5.2.2 p. 19; Table A5 pp. 23-24
bearings.system_side: Each seat token is priced by CU-relevance tier with chair, ranking and vice multipliers. The rule has no party or chamber input, and the committee score feeds the Influence pillar at 40% (per compute_pillars docstring).
bearings.code_ref: fec/engine/committee_scores.py:125-127 (BASE tiers, SUBF, KLEAD); 143-171 seat_weights; 173-186 compute (score = (membership+leadership)/2)
bearings.transfer_conditions: Senate rows only (about 100 senators; the 533 total is not from the paper). Paper calls the evidence suggestive (p. 18). Only Environment and Commerce have reported t-stats; Budget and Rules differences rest on SD gaps with no test. Supports only that seat selection differs by party, not the tier weights or any power claim.
bearings.verifier_note: Table A5 Environment and Commerce figures reproduce exactly (diff, t, SD diff). Softened: the paper says possible discipline, not established (p. 19), and the bearing adds that seats do not reflect structural power, which the paper does not argue. Code constants verified. The analyst omitted that compute() averages membership and leadership.

bearings.paper_claim: Committees differ in common value. Rules, Finance, Governmental Affairs and Appropriations are the most sought after even after excluding the most senior members. In the Republican reduced-form model, Finance and Appropriations have large common value and small idiosyncratic spread, while Constituency committees such as Small Business have lower common value. Sample: 426 assignments, 25 committees, 97 senators, 104th-114th.
bearings.paper_location: Sec. 5.2.3 p. 19; Sec. 5.3 pp. 19-20; Table A5 (Small Business R N=31, D N=18); Tables A6-A8 pp. 24-25; fn. 22 p. 20
bearings.system_side: Every Small Business seat token reads [Highly] on the live sheet (74 of 74, per the committee_scores docstring), and the override that forced it was removed. Seat weight encodes CU relevance only, with no prestige or competitiveness term.
bearings.code_ref: fec/engine/committee_scores.py:45-57 (docstring, Small Business override removed); 125-127 BASE and KLEAD
bearings.transfer_conditions: Tables A7 and A8 numeric cells are garbled in extraction, so the lower-common-value claim for Small Business is verified only as text, not numerically. Republican Senate 1995-2017 only. Use as a validity caveat, not a re-tiering input.
bearings.verifier_note: Named committees and the Small Business N values reproduce from text and Table A5. Softened: the numeric claims rest on Table A7 and A8 cells the extraction cannot show, and Table A6 is partly garbled. The 74-of-74 count comes from the code docstring and was not counted against the sheet.

bearings.paper_claim: Freshman Senate Democrats list Prestige committees as first choice 8% less often than non-freshmen (p=0.15, Frisch-Kelly 1947-1995), consistent with strategic hedging under the Boston mechanism. Republican freshmen show no such gap (p=0.80, Dole archive, first choices only, 91st and 103rd Congresses). The paper treats Democratic strategic reporting as a prediction it cannot test (Prediction 1).
bearings.paper_location: Sec. 5.2.1 p. 19; Figure 1 p. 18; Figure A1 p. 25; Sec. 5.1 p. 18; Prediction 1 p. 9
bearings.system_side: The cell gate lowers Champion or Defender to Ally unless the member authored or original-cosponsored the bill (path A) or has a CU-aligned final-passage vote (path V). Path J is not in cap_uncorroborated, which checks only A and V.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Senate Democrats, descriptive, 1947-1995. The 8 percent gap is not significant at conventional levels (p=0.15). Supports excluding seat-holding as corroboration of an action; says nothing about markup or floor votes.
bearings.verifier_note: The 8 percent figure, p=0.15 and p=0.80 reproduce. Softened: the bearing states that Democratic requests are strategic, but the paper only predicts this and says it cannot test Prediction 1. That seats are not member-chosen costly actions is the analyst's inference. Path J removal rationale is not in the code. Proposition 1 is on p. 15, not p. 16.

related.why: Porter et al. (PNAS 2005) map House committee shared-membership networks. Thakur's account of party-specific seat allocation bears on whether such ties reflect member choice or mechanism. Item exists with text; link is topical.

Verified: Huneeus and Kim use politicians' committee assignments as an instrument, assuming firms cannot influence committee membership. Thakur's finding that placement follows party mechanisms bears on that exogeneity assumption.

Gaynor studies caucus membership and party leaders' donations to members. Thakur models party control of seat allocation through a different channel. The link is topical only; the insulation framing in the source note was not found in the text.

summary_issues: Summary says Republicans work in practice like TTC/YRMH-IGYT. The paper says a pure seniority SD is strategyproof but not individually rational (Table 3), and that Republicans seem to use TTC/YRMH-IGYT in practice (Sec. 3.5.1 p. 13). Hedge it as seems.

Summary reports the Republican p=0.80 gap without saying it is first-choice only, from 91st and 103rd Congress archive data, because 76 percent of non-freshman Republicans rank one choice (Figure A1 note).

Summary and extraction call Prediction 2(c) significant for Budget and Rules. Table A5 shows mean differences of -0.33 (t -0.14) and -1.62 (t -0.56) and only SD gaps of -6.43 and -4.05 with no test reported. Government Affairs has one star and t=1.76.
Summary gives the Frisch-Kelly window as 1947-1995 (80th-103rd Congress), but the Figure 1 caption says 81st to 103rd. Table A4 is labelled 81st to 103rd.
Summary states cross-party gaps point to party discipline. The paper says possible, and the comparison assumes equal true-preference distributions across parties (p. 19).
Summary says freshmen hedge away from Prestige committees. The paper says this is consistent with hedging and the gap is not significant at conventional levels (p=0.15).

Summary figures not from the paper: 533 total members, the 40 percent Influence weight (verified only in the compute_pillars docstring), path J removal rationale (not in code), and the claim that Paul's note is not stale (no paul_entries supplied, so not verifiable).
Proposition 1 is on p. 15, not p. 16, in both the extraction and the rel bearing.
Related link anon-nd-house-committee-requests was dropped: the source has no extracted text and unverified metadata, so the same-data claim cannot be checked.
Tables A6, A7 and A8 are partly garbled in extraction. Any numeric claim drawn from their cells is unverified.
Claim that Democrats' tie-breaking votes are secret and unobserved rests on the Schneider quote in fn. 12 and fn. 21, not a direct observation; acceptable as paraphrase but not a data finding.
